#
# Seed corpus for the DHCPv4 client receive-path fuzz harness, one seed
# per line as "<name> <hex>". gen_corpus.py turns this file into the
# directory of binary seeds libFuzzer wants.
#
# The seeds are hex rather than files because a DHCP message is dense
# with zero bytes - the fixed header, SNAME and FILE fields are almost
# entirely padding - and git calls a file binary as soon as it contains
# a NUL, which the tree does not accept.
#
# Every seed is the DHCP message body: the fixed header (op, htype,
# hlen, xid, ..., chaddr), SNAME, FILE, the magic cookie and the option
# stream, exactly what src/main.c hands to net_recv_data() after the
# IPv4 and UDP headers. The harness overwrites xid and chaddr at
# injection time, so both are left zero/placeholder here; op=2 (BOOT
# REPLY), htype=1, hlen=6 and the chaddr placeholder already match the
# dummy driver's fixed MAC, so a seed reaches dhcpv4_parse_options()
# without the harness needing to touch anything but xid.

# The OFFER lifted from tests/net/dhcpv4/client/src/main.c, byte for
# byte: header + SNAME + FILE + cookie + a run of common options
# (subnet mask, renewal/rebinding/lease time, server id, router, domain
# name, DNS servers, domain search, NetBIOS servers, encapsulated
# vendor-specific option 43 with an oversized inner option, and POP3
# server) ending in the 0xff marker. Exercises the common decode path
# plus three vendor-specific (option 43) edge cases in one seed.
offer 

# The ACK lifted the same way, message type 5, otherwise the same
# option set as the OFFER above (order differs slightly, matching the
# server's real encoding).
ack 

# NAK: message type 6, no other options. Exercises dhcpv4_handle_reply's
# NAK branch, which the OFFER/ACK seeds above never reach.
nak 

# Option 1 (subnet mask) declares a 4-byte payload but the message ends
# two bytes in, and it is the last thing in the buffer, no 0xff marker
# either. Exercises the bounds check dhcpv4_parse_options relies on
# when an option's declared length runs past what is left to read.
opt_length_overrun 

# Option 1 (subnet mask) with a declared length of zero, followed by
# the end marker. Exercises a zero-length option on a code path that
# otherwise expects a fixed 4-byte value.
opt_zero_length 

# One well-formed option (subnet mask) and then the buffer simply ends,
# with no 0xff end-of-options marker. Exercises the loop exit path when
# net_pkt_read_u8() runs out of data instead of seeing DHCPV4_OPTIONS_END.
no_end_marker 

# Option 43 (encapsulated vendor-specific) declares an outer length of
# 2, holding one inner sub-option (0xfe) whose own declared length
# (0x10 = 16) runs past the end of the outer option's 2-byte payload.
# Exercises the nested length check inside the option-43 decoder.
vendor_bad_inner_length 

# Option 15 (domain name), length 8, ASCII "test.com". Exercises the
# harness's plain option callback (registered for this option), whose
# 4-byte buffer is shorter than this option's declared length -
# proving the callback relies on the MIN(cb->max_length, length) clamp
# rather than an always-big-enough buffer.
plain_callback_domain_name 

# Option 43 (encapsulated vendor-specific), outer length 6, holding one
# well-formed inner option: code 0x09 (the harness's registered vendor
# callback code), inner length 4, value aabbccdd. The counterpart to
# vendor_bad_inner_length above: this one is well-formed and exercises
# the harness's vendor-specific option callback.
vendor_callback_hit 

# Option 1 (subnet mask) declaring sixteen bytes, with sixteen bytes
# behind it, against the four byte address the decoder reads it into.
# This is the input the option's fixed length check exists for, and the
# seed the negative control in README.rst names.
opt_subnet_mask_oversize
